m1.title: Bookkeeper — The Service & The System
m1.desc: What we promise, what the board shows, and the disciplines that make both true: cadence, matrix, attestation, follow-ups, ceremony, checklists, playbooks, access.

lessons.title: What we sell, tiers, and what a promise costs
lessons.html:
We keep books for small businesses that run on CloudERP.One — only those. One platform means the skills you build on client one apply exactly to client forty; we sell depth, not adaptability. The work is remote: we hold read-only bank access, post into the client's own ERP site, reconcile, and deliver statements through their portal room.

A client exists for us the moment Customer.accounting_services = "On Board"; the fee lives in Customer.accounting_fees. From that flag the system builds their room, their cadence, and their onboarding runbook overnight. There is no off-boarding state — engagements are built to last.

The tier is the contract, rendered. Core service (every client): postings current, bank reconciliation, monthly financial statements. Optional, per client, ticked in their setup: PAYE remittance, VAT return, WHT remittance, quarterly stock take. Read what the tier means commercially with three scenarios:

  1. Cascade Foods has VAT ticked; you're busy and their VAT cell goes red. That's a paid, promised statutory filing missed — penalty exposure lands on the client, blame lands on us, and the red cell was visible to everyone for days beforehand. Tier items are not decorations.
  2. Harmattan Logistics has NO statutory ticks, and their MD emails asking you to "quickly file our VAT". You do not quietly do it. Unpaid statutory work done once becomes expected forever, and worse — done without engagement terms, an error in it is our liability with no fee behind it. The answer: "happy to — let me have our team add statutory filing to your service; it takes one setting and a fee adjustment." Then management decides.
  3. Bellamy Stores' cell shows ↻ Sep under Stock take in July. Subscribed, dormant — quarterly items live only in Mar/Jun/Sep/Dec periods. Distinguish this from "—", which means not in the tier at all.

Fees are visible only to books managers — the matrix shows you everything operational and nothing financial. That is deliberate; your job needs due dates, not price lists.

DRILL: A prospect asks your colleague "so you'll handle all our taxes?" during onboarding. The tier picker shows nothing ticked. What's wrong with "yes, of course"? — It promises unpriced statutory liability; the correct move is the tier conversation, then the ticks, then the promise.

lessons.title: The cadence and the calendar — computing what's due
lessons.html:
Every deliverable's due date is computed, not remembered, against our working calendar (Duty Settings: Mon–Fri unless changed). Learn the three bases by computing them:

DeliverableRuleJuly 2026 period → due
Bank journals posted & currentLast working day of periodFri 31 Jul
Bank reconciliation3rd working day of next monthWed 5 Aug (Mon 3rd = 1st wd, Tue = 2nd, Wed = 3rd)
Financial statements5th working day of next monthFri 7 Aug
PAYE remittanceFixed day: 10th of next month, snap BACKWARDMon 10 Aug (a working day — stays)
VAT / WHTFixed day: 21st of next month, snap BACKWARDFri 21 Aug (stays)

The snap-backward rule is the one to internalise: when the 21st falls on a Saturday (Nov 2026), the due date becomes Friday the 20th — never Monday the 23rd. Statutory deadlines are met early; a weekend is never an excuse for late. Working-day rules (statements) count only workdays, so a public-holiday-heavy month genuinely moves the date — trust the matrix's computed date over your mental arithmetic.

Spawning is automatic. A daily job syncs newly on-boarded customers and opens the current period: every client × every core type + their ticked optionals, each instance pre-assigned to the client's default bookkeeper. You never create the month's work; you inherit it, dated.

Late is computed too: a cell whose due date has passed without Delivered goes red with ⚠ — on the matrix, in the pulse strip's count, and in the evening digest. There is no "I'll mark it late" and no "nobody noticed". The board notices structurally.

DRILL: October 2026 — the 21st is a Wednesday, but suppose the 5th working day of November must be computed and Mon 2 Nov is a public holiday added to settings. Count it: Tue 3 = 1st, Wed 4 = 2nd, Thu 5 = 3rd, Fri 6 = 4th, Mon 9 = 5th. Statements due Mon 9 Nov. The matrix already knows; the drill is trusting why.

lessons.title: Reading the matrix like a triage nurse
lessons.html:
The Matrix tab is one row per client, one column per deliverable, one period. Reading it fast is a skill; here is a full row, decoded:

Bellamy Stores · 📮 posted thru 07-24 · lag 2wd (amber) · Bank journals ◐ · Bank rec · due 08-05 · Financial statements · due 08-07 · PAYE — · VAT ✓ 08-21 · Stock take ↻ Sep

  • The amber 📮 chip: the books trail reality by two working days — inside tolerance, worth closing today.
  • ◐ postings in progress; · rec and statements pending (normal mid-cycle); the dates under each cell are computed due dates.
  • PAYE "—": not in Bellamy's tier. If Bellamy asks about PAYE, that's the Lesson-1 tier conversation.
  • VAT ✓ already Delivered for the period — early, good.
  • Red cell anywhere = past due; 👁 = sitting with a reviewer; ✓✓ = client has acknowledged receipt.

Cells are doors. Clicking one opens the deliverable: its close checklist with progress, and status / assignee / reviewer / notes, all prefilled. The client's name column carries the 📖 playbook and (for managers) the fee.

The header serves every tab at once: the period selector ‹ 2026-07 › drives Matrix, Register, Follow-ups and the manager tabs together — investigating May means setting May once. The pulse strip above is the unit's vital signs: clients · done/total · late · neglect · awaiting-clients — read it before your first click each morning; it tells you where today's triage is.

DRILL: Pulse reads: 6 clients · 14/24 done · 1 late ⚠ · 1 neglected ⚠ · 📨 3❓ 2📎. In what order do you look? — Neglect first (a client nobody has touched), the late cell second (a broken promise aging), the follow-ups third (clients are waiting on us). Done-count last; it's yesterday's news.

lessons.title: A week on the round — attestation and its ethics
lessons.html:
Once a day, per client, you make a small signed claim: "books posted through [date]" — with optional transaction and query counts and a note. Two taps in the 📅 tab. What follows is a realistic week; live it once here so you never live it badly in production.

Setup: you own Bellamy, Cascade, Harmattan. Monday the 14th: Bellamy posted through Fri 11th (lag 1, green), Cascade through Thu 10th (lag 2, amber), Harmattan through Wed 9th (lag 3, red — your leave cover attested nothing).

Monday. Worst first — the board is a triage list, not a menu. Session tagged Harmattan; post Thursday-through-today; attest "posted through 14-07 · 41 tx · 1 query". Register cell goes ●, chip green. Then Cascade, then Bellamy. 18:00 digest: all covered. Nobody thinks about you — that is the goal state.

Tuesday — the trap. Cascade's MD demands a creditor analysis; it eats the day. At 17:50 you consider skipping the round — "nothing to attest". Wrong twice. (1) You worked Cascade all day: attest Cascade with the same posted-through as yesterday plus a note: "creditor analysis for MD; postings current to 14-07". An unchanged date with a note is honest; a missing attestation is a hole. (2) Bellamy and Harmattan show · today — no flag yet, but streaks have started.

Wednesday — the flag. The MD found more questions; another Cascade-only day. By close, Bellamy and Harmattan each carry 2 silent working days: both rows red, streak "2wd", named in the 18:00 digest to the whole unit. No message arrives, no meeting is called — every colleague simply saw it. Visibility, not escalation, is the system's entire theory of accountability.

Thursday — recovery, honestly. You clear both backlogs through Wednesday and attest. Chips: posted "through Wednesday" on Thursday = lag 1, green. Note what you must NOT do: attest "through Thursday" to make the chip perfect when you've only posted through Wednesday. The chip is allowed to be amber; the attestation is not allowed to be false. An amber chip says "a day behind"; a false green says "trust me" to a system whose cross-checks (sessions vs claims, and one day the ledger itself) have a long memory.

Friday — the habit. Run the round at a fixed time (16:30 works) so it's a ritual, not a memory test. The week's register reads Mon ●●●, Tue ●··, Wed ●··, Thu ●●●, Fri ●●● — the Tuesday–Wednesday scar is permanent, honest history. Fine. The board doesn't demand perfection; it demands that reality and the record never diverge.

Register glyphs, precisely: ● worked (customer-tagged session) + attested · ◐ worked, no attestation (finish the ritual) · ◔ attested, no session (a claim without visible presence — expect the question) · · untouched. Future dates in the attestation box are refused outright: you cannot have posted tomorrow's transactions.

DRILL: You attested "through 22-07" yesterday. Today the client sends Monday's missing statement page and you post 6 older transactions. Tonight's attestation? — Still "through 23-07" if today's lines are also in; the older insertions don't break the claim, they fulfil it. Add a note: "6 late-arriving 21-07 tx posted on receipt of statement page."

lessons.title: Follow-ups — the query lifecycle, end to end
lessons.html:
Bookkeeping stalls on unclassifiable transactions and missing documents. Follow-ups turns both into structured, chased, logged objects. Walk one full query lifecycle:

Day 1, 10:15 — posting Bellamy, you hit "CHQ 000451 MUSA ENT ₦230,000", no supplier, no invoice. You post to suspense (M2a craft) and raise the query from 📨: date 09-07, amount 230,000, reference "CHQ 000451 Musa Ent", question: "Could you help us place this cheque to Musa Ent on the 9th — what was it for, and is Musa a supplier we should set up?" Note the shape: help-us-understand, never you-didn't-tell-us.

What Bellamy sees: an amber card on the portal home with an inline answer box, AND an email from books@pangeasuite.com — replying to that email IS answering; the system trims the quoted chain and files the reply as the answer, attributed. Clients who never open the portal can live entirely in email; everything still lands structured.

Day 3, 09:30 — no answer yet. The morning chase notices the query is 2 working days stale and drops ONE gentle line in Bellamy's room chat: "🔔 Gentle reminder: 1 question from your accounting team is awaiting your response." One per room per day, maximum, however many items wait — persistence without nagging, and none of it from your memory.

Day 3, 14:00 — Mr Bellamy replies to the email: "Generator repair, and yes set Musa up." The query flips to Answered (green in your Follow-ups, his name and timestamp on it), the room narrates it. You repost suspense → Repairs & Maintenance, create the supplier, and click ✓ Resolve. Lifecycle closed: Open → Answered → Resolved, every step logged.

Documents run the same rails: the standard monthly set (bank statements, payroll changes — whatever Settings lists) spawns at period open, due early; ad-hoc requests are two fields. Fulfilment by portal upload or email-reply-with-attachment lands identically: the file goes to the Document Hub under "Accounting — received", the request closes, the room narrates. Your 📥 Recently-received list shows who sent what, when, with the file one click away.

DRILL: It's the 26th and you're about to raise 14 queries you accumulated all month. What went wrong, and when? — The queries should have been raised the day each was hit (your daily round even counts queries-raised to encourage it). A query raised on the 5th is answered by the 8th; 14 on the 26th is a late close, self-inflicted.

lessons.title: One close, walked — review gate and ceremony
lessons.html:
Follow Cascade Foods' July statements from last posting to ✓✓. Cascade is a split client: you prepare, Ade reviews.

Aug 4 (2nd wd): postings complete, reconciliation done and filed, suspense zero (the last query resolved Aug 1). You open the Financial statements cell: the checklist appears — payroll booked ☑, accruals ☑, depreciation ☑, VAT/WHT controls reconciled ☑, flux review ☑ (your notes: "COGS +18% — new supplier pricing, MD aware"), PDF to Hub ☑ — six of seven; the seventh is "Reviewer pass complete", which is not yours to tick.

Aug 5: you set the cell to In Review. Ade gets a 👁 push: "Cascade Foods · Financial statements · 2026-07". Your notes flag your one doubt: "director loan repostings in week 3 — please eyeball." Surfacing your own doubts is what makes reviewers trust everything else.

Aug 6: Ade reviews substance — recs to statements, flux against what he knows of Cascade, controls to schedules, your flagged item. One finding comes back: "rent release doubled — March's reversal missing; fix and re-lay the P&L." You fix it, re-file the PDF, note the correction. Ade ticks "Reviewer pass complete" and — because only the reviewer can — sets Delivered. If you'd tried, the system would have refused you by name: the review gate is structural, not courtesy. The room narrates: "📒 Financial statements — 2026-07 is ready for Cascade Foods."

Aug 6, evening: Cascade's portal home shows the 📬 card. Their accountant taps Confirm receipt — the deliverable becomes Acknowledged, timestamped, named; the room narrates; you get the push; your matrix shows ✓✓, one day inside the 5th-working-day promise.

Why each step exists: the checklist makes "done" mean something specific; the gate makes "two people believe this" a fact; the Hub-before-ceremony order means the client is never pointed at an empty shelf; and the acknowledgment timestamp ends every future "we never received our statements" before it begins. Acknowledged can never be set by staff — only the client's own tap creates it, which is exactly what makes it proof.

DRILL: Deadline day, reviewer travelling, statements ready. May you deliver? — Not by yourself; the gate holds. Escalate to a books manager/System Manager early in the day — the override exists for genuine cases like this, and a pattern of overrides gets read for what it is. What you never do is quietly remove the reviewer from the cell to free the button; that edit is logged too, and it reads worse.

lessons.title: Checklists as evidence — what each tick verifies
lessons.html:
A checklist tick is a small signed statement. Ticking without verifying is signing without reading. Here is the Financial statements checklist with what each tick actually asserts:

ItemYour tick asserts
Payroll bookedThe month's payroll journal is posted and the net cleared against the salary payment; liability accounts agree to the payroll schedule.
Accruals & prepayments postedRecurring accruals raised, prior accruals reversed against actuals, prepayment releases per schedule — not "probably".
Depreciation postedAsset-module run verified sane, or manual JE posted from the register — either way, checked.
VAT/WHT controls reconciledControl movements agree to the period's invoice summaries and certificate schedules.
P&L flux reviewEvery material month-on-month movement has a one-sentence explanation, written in the notes.
PDF filed to HubThe pack the client will open is on the shelf, final version, before the ceremony points at it.
Reviewer passReviewer's alone. Never yours.

Ticks are timestamped and named forever. Marking Delivered with open items triggers "n items still open — deliver anyway?" — the system permits the override, and the unticked items remain visible permanently with your name on the delivery. Sometimes the override is right (an item genuinely not applicable this month); when it is, say so in the notes, because silence next to an untick reads as haste.

Statutory deliverables carry no checklist by design — a remittance is filed or it isn't; M3 covers the filing evidence discipline. Checklists are editable per type in the desk: when the unit learns a new failure mode, it becomes a line, and every future period inherits the lesson.

DRILL: You inherit a client mid-month; the previous bookkeeper's June delivery shows 6/7 with "controls reconciled" unticked and no note. What does that tell you to do FIRST this month? — Reconcile June's controls before touching July; an unticked control item is a flagged inheritance, and July's numbers stand on June's.

lessons.title: Playbooks, the access register, and the trust we hold
lessons.html:
The playbook is your duty to colleagues. Every client's 📖 holds four sections; here is what a good one looks like (Bellamy's, abbreviated):

BANKS & STATEMENTS — GTB current (statement emailed by RM ~2nd; chase Tunde 0803… if absent); POS settles next-morning net, commission ~0.55%, clearing acct must zero within 2 days.
KEY CONTACTS — Mr Bellamy (owner; decisions, director-money questions); Chidinma (bookkeeper-side, sends Z-reports; WhatsApp is fine for her, but decisions go in the room).
MONTH PECULIARITIES — salaries 26th; owner pays suppliers personally then reimburses — watch TRF FRM MR BELLAMY both directions; December stock take includes the Surulere store.
ACCESS NOTES — bank read-only via corporate viewer, renewed annually Oct; ERP Accounts role; credentials in the access vault, never in chat.

The test of a playbook: could a competent colleague run this client tomorrow from what's written? Update it the day you learn something a stand-in would need — after the fact means never.

The Access Register is the unit's security posture made showable: every access we hold, one record — type, detail, granted, last reviewed. When a prospect asks "what exactly will you have access to?", the answer is a filtered screen, not an assurance. Registering new access is an onboarding runbook step, and unreviewed entries age visibly.

The trust itself, in rules: read-only means read-only — we watch money move, we never move it; a client asking you to initiate a transfer gets a kind no and a same-day report to management, every time. Client data never leaves its room: no cross-client "benchmarks", no side-channel WhatsApp threads, no dinner stories however nameless. Exports live in the Hub, not in personal archives. The breach that ends a career is rarely dramatic — it's a screenshot to the wrong chat, a laptop left open, a story told well. Boring discipline is the whole game.

DRILL: Write, from memory, the playbook entry your most complicated client would need for the one thing only you currently know about them. If you can't think of one, you've been updating properly — or you haven't been paying attention. Check which.

m2a.title: Bookkeeper — Daily Posting Craft
m2a.desc: Statement to ledger, line by line: the three documents, Nigerian statement anatomy, Payment Entries both directions, journal craft, the worked month, suspense, and clearing accounts.

lessons.title: The three documents and the decision tree
lessons.html:
Every bank line becomes exactly one of three ERPNext documents. The decision is mechanical once you ask the right first question: is there a party (customer/supplier) whose ledger this must touch?

The line is…DocumentWhy
Money from a customer / to a supplierPayment Entry (Receive / Pay), allocated to invoicesThe party's ledger and aging must clear
Between the client's own accountsPayment Entry — Internal TransferTwo bank ledgers move; P&L untouched
Everything else — charges, taxes paid, salaries clearing, corrections, unknownsJournal EntryPure account-to-account movement

The full tree for a debit line: party payment? → Payment Entry (Pay). Own account? → Internal Transfer. Recognisable expense/statutory? → Journal Entry. Unrecognisable? → Journal Entry to Suspense + query today (Lesson 7). Mirror it for credits, with one extra rule: unidentified money in is NEVER Sales (Lesson 7 explains the damage).

Two invariants regardless of document: (1) Posting Date = statement date, never today's — the ledger reconstructs the month as it happened; posting July lines with August dates is how reconciliations die. (2) Remarks reconstruct the transaction for a stranger: date, counterparty, what-for, statement reference. House narration format: "[Counterparty] — [what] — [ref], stmt [dd-mm]". "Being payment" is not a narration; your reviewer, your future reconciling self, and an eventual auditor are the audience.

Work account by account, date order, no gaps. A line skipped "for later" is a reconciliation wound; a line you can't place goes to suspense with its query the same day — skipping and suspensing are opposites.

DRILL: "TRF TO ACCESS OWN ACCT ₦2,000,000" — which document, and what does P&L show after? Internal Transfer; P&L shows nothing. If you feel the urge to touch an expense account, re-read the line.

lessons.title: Reading a Nigerian bank statement — line anatomy
lessons.html:
Statement narrations are compressed telegrams. Learn the dialects:

PatternUsually meansPosting instinct
NIBSS/POS SETTLEMENT [date]Previous day's card sales, net of commissionClear POS clearing acct; commission to Bank Charges (L8)
TRF FRM / NIP FRM [name]/[ref]Inward transfer; name + ref are your allocation cluesPayment Entry Receive if the name maps to a customer
TRF TO / NIP TO [name]Outward transferPayment Entry Pay if supplier; else JE by nature
CHQ [number] [payee]Cheque clearedAs outward; the cheque number goes in Reference No
USSD AIRTIME / [phone]Airtime bought from the accountExpense JE — and if frequent/personal-looking, a query about policy
SMS ALERT / MAINT FEE / COTBank charges familyBank Charges, the moment you meet them
STAMP DUTY₦50 EMTL per qualifying creditStamp Duty/Charges expense; often many tiny lines — post, don't hoard
WHT ON INTEREST / VAT ON FEETax the bank deducted at sourceWHT: asset (credit vs tax); VAT on fees: part of the charge per convention
REVERSAL / RVSL [ref]An earlier line undoneFind and reverse YOUR posting of the original — never post a reversal blind
LOAN REPAYMENT / PRINCIPAL+INTFacility servicingSplit: principal to loan liability, interest to finance cost — the offer letter (playbook!) gives the split

Reversals deserve fear and respect: a REVERSAL line means the bank undid something. If you already posted the original, post its mirror and cross-reference both remarks ("reverses JE-00231"). If the original AND its reversal both appear before you posted either, post neither — but note both on the reconciliation so the statement still walks.

Names lie slightly: transfers arrive under personal names for corporate customers ("ADEBAYO OLUFEMI J" paying for Adebayo Ventures), abbreviations, or the payer's BANK's shorthand. The playbook accumulates these aliases; when a name is genuinely new, it's a query, not a guess (L7).

DRILL: "NIP FRM OKONKWO C/INV0244PART ₦300,000" — decode every element: NIP inward transfer, payer alias Okonkwo C (check playbook aliases), reference declares itself a PART payment of invoice 0244. Document: Payment Entry Receive, partial allocation, remarks noting 'part'.

lessons.title: Payment Entry (Receive) — fields, and allocation with numbers
lessons.html:
The bread-and-butter document, field by field. Path: Accounting → Payment Entry → New.

  1. Payment Type: Receive · Party Type: Customer · Party: Adebayo Ventures — on selection, the References table loads their outstanding invoices.
  2. Posting Date: the statement date. Account Paid To: GTB Current (the ERP bank account mapped to the real one — the playbook lists the mapping).
  3. Paid Amount: exactly the statement credit.
  4. References: allocate to invoices until Allocated = Paid. Reference No / Date: the transfer ref and its date — reconciliation matches on these. Remarks: house format.

Now the allocation cases, with numbers. Adebayo owes: INV-0231 ₦500,000 (May) · INV-0244 ₦800,000 (June) · INV-0252 ₦450,000 (July).

Case 1 — referenced payment. ₦500,000 arrives "/INV 0231". Allocate 500,000 to INV-0231 exactly, even though it's not the only old invoice. The reference is the customer's instruction; honour it.

Case 2 — unreferenced lump. ₦1,300,000 arrives, no reference. Oldest-first: 500,000 → 0231, 800,000 → 0244. Both close; 0252 stays open. Remarks name the rule used: "unreferenced — allocated oldest-first per policy".

Case 3 — the shortfall. ₦1,235,000 arrives "/INV0231+0244" — ₦65,000 short of the 1,300,000 those invoices total. Adebayo is a company: the first suspect is WHT withheld at source (5% of the ₦1,300,000 service value = ₦65,000 — it fits). Allocate the full 1,300,000 across both invoices; the ₦65,000 difference posts in the same entry as a deduction to the WHT receivable (asset) account — pending the credit note/certificate, which becomes a document request. If the numbers DON'T fit a WHT rate, the shortfall is a dispute or error: allocate what the money truly covers and query the difference. Never invent a discount or write-off to force a fit.

Case 4 — the overpayment/deposit. ₦2,000,000 arrives against ₦1,750,000 outstanding. Allocate 1,750,000; the ₦250,000 remainder stays as an unallocated advance on Adebayo's ledger, by intention, with remarks saying so ("₦250,000 advance per MD — allocate to August order"). An advance is a known thing awaiting its invoice — it is not suspense.

Case 5 — bank charge netted. Statement credit ₦498,950 for a ₦500,000 invoice; ₦1,050 was the payer-side charge passed on. The customer paid the gross: receive 500,000, allocate fully, and the 1,050 posts as Bank Charges in the entry's deductions — Adebayo's ledger must clear completely.

DRILL: ₦940,500 arrives against a single ₦990,000 invoice from a corporate customer. Does WHT explain it? 5% of 990,000 = 49,500; 990,000 − 49,500 = 940,500. Yes — full allocation + ₦49,500 to WHT receivable + a request for the certificate.

lessons.title: Payment Entry (Pay), on-account, and the missing-invoice stop rule
lessons.html:
The mirror direction: Payment Type Pay, Party a supplier, Account Paid From the bank, allocate against purchase invoices. Same fields, same invariants, one new discipline:

The stop rule. "TRF TO KOLAWOLE DISTRIB/PO 118 ₦1,850,000" — but no purchase invoice for PO 118 exists in the system. STOP. This is not a posting problem; it is a missing-document problem, and the two must never be confused. The moves, in order: (1) raise a document request for the supplier invoice, same day; (2) post the payment on-account to Kolawole (a Pay entry with no allocation), remarks naming PO 118; (3) when the invoice arrives and is entered, allocate the on-account payment against it. What you never do: fabricate a purchase invoice to allocate against, or dump the payment to an expense guess — both create a ledger that lies about what the client owes.

Supplier-side WHT — the direction flips. When the CLIENT withholds from a supplier's invoice: invoice ₦1,000,000, WHT 5%, cash out ₦950,000. The Pay entry allocates the full 1,000,000 against the invoice; the ₦50,000 difference posts to WHT payable (liability) — the client now holds government money until remittance (M3's territory to file; yours to hold correctly). Compare Lesson 3, Case 3: withheld FROM us = asset; withheld BY us = liability. Direction is everything; a bookkeeper who confuses them creates phantom income or phantom expense.

Part-payments to suppliers mirror customer partials: allocate exactly what was paid; the invoice stays open; remarks say "part 1 of 2 per terms" when you know the plan (playbook again).

Recurring standing payments (rent by standing order, loan direct debits): the playbook lists them with their split; posting is mechanical. A standing payment that STOPS appearing is also information — note it, and query if unexpected.

DRILL: Payment ₦712,500 to a consultant whose invoice reads ₦750,000. The withholding rate implied? 37,500/750,000 = 5%... but consultants/professional services commonly withhold at a different rate — check the schedule in M3/house table before posting the split. The drill's real lesson: the ARITHMETIC identifies withholding; the RATE TABLE confirms it. When they disagree, query.

lessons.title: Journal Entry craft — charges, statutory payments, corrections
lessons.html:
Everything party-less runs through Journal Entry: Accounting → Journal Entry → New, rows of account/debit/credit, total balanced, posting date = statement date, remarks per house format.

The charges family — post on sight, never hoard:

LineDrCr
SMS ALERT ₦1,254Bank Charges 1,254GTB Current 1,254
STAMP DUTY ₦50 (×many)Stamp Duty/Charges 50GTB Current 50
WHT ON INTEREST ₦2,100 (bank deducted)WHT Receivable 2,100Interest Income 2,100 (grossing up the credit you also received)

Statutory payments out clear their control accounts, never expense: "FIRS VAT PAYMENT JUN ₦861,000" → Dr VAT Payable 861,000, Cr GTB Current 861,000. If the control didn't hold ₦861,000 the moment before, something upstream is wrong — that's an M2b controls investigation, not a plug. Same pattern for PAYE and pension remittances against their liability accounts.

Corrections have one honest shape: reverse the wrong entry (ERPNext: the entry's Reverse action, or a mirror JE cross-referencing it), then post the right one. Never "fix" by editing history that reconciliation already saw, and never post a net-difference adjustment that hides what happened — remarks on both entries tell the story: "reverses JE-00231 (wrong account); correct posting JE-00232."

Narration examples, good and bad: ✗ "Being bank charges" · ✓ "GTB SMS alert charges June, stmt 04-07" · ✗ "Correction" · ✓ "Reverses JE-00231 — generator repair posted to fuel in error; see JE-00232". The good ones cost ten seconds and save an hour each at review, reconciliation, and audit.

DRILL: Interest income line: statement shows CREDIT ₦39,900 and a separate DEBIT "WHT ON INTEREST ₦2,100". Post it as one economic event: Dr GTB 39,900 + Dr WHT Receivable 2,100, Cr Interest Income 42,000. The client earned 42,000; the statement just delivered it in two lines.

lessons.title: The worked month — twelve lines of Bellamy Stores
lessons.html:
Bellamy Stores Ltd: retail, standard tier + VAT, one GTB current account. Playbook notes: salaries the 26th; the owner sometimes pays suppliers personally and reimburses himself; POS settles next-morning net. Twelve July lines — post them all, using everything so far.

1 — POS settlement. Daily sales already posted to POS Clearing when Z-reports were entered; the settlement clears it: Dr GTB 412,350, Cr POS Clearing 412,350. Short of the clearing balance? The gap is POS commission → Bank Charges in the same JE, clearing still zeroes. A clearing account that won't zero within 2 days = query (missing Z-report) or playbook gap (undocumented fee).

2 — referenced receipt. Payment Entry Receive, Adebayo, allocate 500,000 to INV-0231 exactly (L3 Case 1).

3 — charge. JE per L5. Post it now, not "later".

4 — supplier payment, invoice present? If the PO 118 purchase invoice is in: Pay + allocate. If not: stop rule (L4) — on-account + document request, never a fabricated invoice.

5 — unknown payee. No supplier, no invoice: Dr Suspense 230,000, Cr GTB — and the query goes out the same hour (L7 walks its life).

6 — unknown money IN. Dr GTB 150,000, Cr Suspense. Never Sales: if this is a customer deposit, crediting Sales corrupts VAT and the customer's ledger simultaneously. Query with the ref.

7 — own-account move. Internal Transfer, 1,000,000, both bank ledgers move, P&L silent. The classic error is posting one side; the OTHER account's reconciliation fails next month — the expensive way to find out.

8 — stamp duty. JE, ₦50, on sight.

9 — part payment. Receive 300,000, allocate against INV-0244, invoice stays open, remarks say "part".

10 — VAT paid. Dr VAT Payable 861,000, Cr GTB. The control held exactly this; if it didn't, M2b's diagnosis lesson is your next stop before anything else.

11 — salaries. Dr Salaries Payable/net-pay control 1,420,000, Cr GTB. The 26th's payroll journal (M2b) already booked gross to expense and split the liabilities; the bank clears only the NET. If you feel the urge to debit Salary Expense here, the payroll journal is missing — different problem, fix that.

12 — the owner's money. Playbook warned you. ₦750,000 FROM Mr Bellamy could be: reimbursement flowing the wrong way (no — reimbursement would be a debit), capital introduced, or a director loan. The balance-sheet story differs completely between those; directors' money is never guessed: Dr GTB, Cr Suspense, query to Mr Bellamy naming the ref, repost on answer (capital → equity; loan → director loan liability).

Count the craft: 2 Receives, 1 Pay (or on-account), 1 Internal Transfer, 4 JEs, 3 suspense+query. Tonight's attestation "posted through 28-07" is TRUE — including the suspensed lines, because suspense-with-query IS posted.

DRILL: Re-post line 12 assuming Mr Bellamy answers "it's a loan, I'll take it back in October." Dr Suspense 750,000, Cr Director Loan — Mr Bellamy 750,000; remarks reference the query and his answer; October's repayment will clear the loan account, not expense.

lessons.title: Suspense and the query — the honest parking bay, end to end
lessons.html:
Suspense holds a transaction while its question is being answered — nothing else. The lifecycle, using Bellamy line 5:

  1. Post to suspense the moment you meet the unknown (Dr Suspense 230,000, Cr GTB) — the bank ledger stays current, which is what your attestation claims.
  2. Raise the query the same day — date, amount, "CHQ 000451 Musa Ent", the help-shaped question. Suspense without a query is procrastination with an account code; the pairing is what makes it honest.
  3. The system chases (one gentle room reminder per day once stale) — persistence is not your memory's job.
  4. Answer lands ("generator repair; set Musa up") → repost: Dr Repairs & Maintenance 230,000, Cr Suspense 230,000, remarks referencing the query; create the supplier; Resolve the query.

The three iron rules: suspense clears to ZERO before statements — the FS checklist cannot honestly complete over material unexplained balances; an item genuinely unresolvable by close despite the chase is an explicit disclosed decision with the reviewer (reclassify on best evidence with a note, or hold with the client informed) — never a silent rollover; and suspense is for unknowns only — a customer advance awaiting its invoice is a known thing on the customer's ledger, not suspense.

Directionality: unknown money OUT sits as a suspense debit; unknown money IN as a suspense credit. A suspense account carrying BOTH directions un-netted is normal mid-month and must be worked item by item — never net a debit-unknown against a credit-unknown to "tidy" the balance; they are different questions.

The health read: a growing suspense balance is the single clearest sign of an engagement drifting — visible to your reviewer, and honestly, the first thing a good reviewer checks. Keep the bay near-empty and the queries flowing daily, and month-end becomes a formality.

DRILL: July 30th, statements due Aug 7. Suspense holds: ₦230,000 (answered yesterday — repost today), ₦150,000 (query 5 days old, chased twice, silent), ₦18,500 (met this morning, query just raised). What does honest close look like? Repost the first now; escalate the second to the client by name via the room + reviewer disclosure if still silent at close; the third will likely resolve in the chase window — and if not, it's small: reviewer decision with a note. Zero silent rollovers.

lessons.title: Clearing accounts and cash businesses — POS, Z-reports, floats
lessons.html:
Retail clients live on card machines and cash tills; clearing accounts are how their sales meet their bank truthfully.

The POS clearing pattern. Sales day: the Z-report (till summary) posts Dr POS Clearing / Dr Cash-in-till, Cr Sales, Cr VAT Output — the day's revenue recognised on the day it happened. Settlement morning: the NIBSS batch arrives net; Dr GTB + Dr Bank Charges (commission), Cr POS Clearing — the clearing zeroes for that day. The clearing account is therefore a timing device with a built-in alarm: any balance older than ~2 settlement days is a missing Z-report (query the client), a failed settlement (query the bank narration), or an undocumented fee (update the playbook).

Cash rounds: till cash → banking. Z-report already debited Cash-in-till; the deposit line "CASH DEP" posts Dr GTB, Cr Cash-in-till. The till account's balance should equal the float plus undeposited takings — a persistent unexplained excess or shortage is a variance: post small ones to a Cash Over/Short expense per house threshold, and query patterns (same till, same day-of-week) because patterns are process problems or worse, and our statements shouldn't quietly absorb either.

Multiple settlement channels (POS terminal A, terminal B, transfer-on-delivery apps): one clearing account per channel if volumes justify — the alarm only works if channels don't muddy each other. The playbook lists the client's channels, their fee rates, and their settlement rhythms; when a new channel appears on the statement unannounced, that's a playbook update AND a query ("we see settlements from X — new till?").

What this lesson protects: revenue completeness. Sales recognised from Z-reports and PROVEN by settlements is an assertion chain an auditor can walk; sales recognised from "whatever hit the bank" undercounts card fees, miscounts VAT, and collapses the day cash goes missing. The clearing discipline is the difference.

DRILL: POS Clearing shows ₦380,000 aged 4 days. The playbook says settlements are next-morning. Three hypotheses in order of likelihood, and the action for each? Missing Z-report (ask for it); settlement failure/hold (find the absent NIBSS line, query with dates); a new terminal settling elsewhere (ask, then playbook + possibly a new clearing account). All three start with a query TODAY — the alarm rang.

m2b.desc: Reconciliation with numbers, accruals and reversals, prepayment schedules, the full payroll journal, control accounts diagnosed, flux review, and the statements pack.

lessons.title: Bank reconciliation — a worked agreement
lessons.html:
Reconciliation proves the posting month worked: the bank's closing balance agreed to the ledger, every difference listed and explicable. Work one:

Bellamy, GTB Current, 31 July. Statement closing balance: ₦4,481,204. ERP bank ledger balance: ₦4,213,450. Difference: ₦267,754 — now we explain every kobo of it.

ERPNext path: Accounting → Bank Reconciliation Tool — select the account, enter statement date and closing balance; the tool lists unreconciled ledger entries to match against statement lines (or clear by date). Working it produces:

Reconciling item₦Nature
Ledger balance per ERP4,213,450
+ CHQ 000455 to Eze Bros, issued 29-07, not yet presented310,000Unpresented cheque — will clear in August
− Customer NIP received 31-07 20:41, posted by us, credited by bank 01-08(41,000)Timing: late-day value
− July COT-style maintenance fee on statement, not yet posted(1,246)Our miss — post it NOW (Dr Bank Charges), then it stops reconciling

Three of the four rows above teach the three species of difference: genuine timing (unpresented cheques, late-day credits — listed, aged, expected to self-clear), our misses (unposted lines discovered here — post them immediately; a reconciliation that "carries" postable items is a posting list wearing a reconciliation's clothes), and — not present this month, happily — errors (wrong amounts, one-sided transfers, duplicates: reverse-and-repost per M2a L5).

The aging rule: unpresented/uncleared items older than one month are not timing anymore — a 6-week-old cheque is stale-dating, a duplicate, or a payment the payee never got. Investigate, reverse, or query; never roll forward silently. And a difference you cannot explain is NEVER plugged — it goes to suspense with a query and a note on the reconciliation saying exactly that.

Close the loop: reconcile per account, every account in the tier; file the reconciliation to the Hub (the checklist tick's evidence); and read the meta-signal — if reconciliation keeps discovering unposted lines, your daily rhythm failed and your attested posting lag was overstated. Fix the habit, not just the month.

DRILL: Statement ₦2,105,300; ledger ₦2,145,300; one unpresented cheque ₦65,000; one unposted charge you find, ₦X. Solve: ledger 2,145,300 + 65,000 unpresented should equal statement + X unposted... Work it: 2,145,300 − 2,105,300 = 40,000 gap; unpresented explains +65,000 the other way → the unposted charge X = 25,000 (Dr Bank Charges). Post it, re-run, agree.

lessons.title: Accruals and reversals — two months, one truth
lessons.html:
Cash postings say what happened; accruals make the statements tell the truth about the period. The mechanism is a pair of entries across two months — walk one:

July 31: Bellamy's PHCN/IKEDC bill for July hasn't arrived (it never does before the 10th). Estimate from the playbook's pattern (last 3 months: 118k, 124k, 121k → accrue ₦121,000):

31-07 JournalDrCr
Electricity Expense121,000
Accrued Expenses (liability)121,000

August 1 (or on posting the actual): the accrual REVERSES — ERPNext journal entries support reversal on a date; use it rather than remembering:

01-08 ReversalDrCr
Accrued Expenses121,000
Electricity Expense121,000

August 12: the real bill lands: ₦126,300, paid by transfer. Post it normally (Dr Electricity 126,300, Cr Bank). Net effect across the two months: July shows 121,000 (the estimate — close enough, and honest), August shows 126,300 − 121,000 = 5,300 (the estimate's true-up). Nothing doubled, nothing missed — that is the whole choreography, and skipping the reversal is the classic way electricity appears twice in August.

What gets accrued monthly (the playbook lists each client's set): utilities billed in arrears, audit/professional fees relating to the year, interest on facilities between charge dates, salaries where the pay date crosses month end. What does NOT: amounts already invoiced (those are payables, not accruals) and wild guesses — an accrual needs a basis (pattern, contract, rate); "roughly 200k" with no basis is noise wearing a liability's clothes, and your reviewer will ask for the basis.

Income accrues too when the client has earned but not yet invoiced (rare in retail, common in services): Dr Accrued Income (asset), Cr Revenue — same reversal choreography when the invoice is raised.

DRILL: You forgot July's reversal; August now shows Electricity 247,300. The flux review (L6) catches the doubling — what's the fix? Post the missed reversal dated in August with remarks explaining, bringing August to 126,300 − 121,000 = 5,300... wait — the reversal alone brings it to 126,300; the true-up view (5,300 above run-rate) is what flux then shows and explains. Fix, re-lay, note. The deeper fix: use dated auto-reversal so memory isn't a control.

lessons.title: Prepayments — building and running the schedule
lessons.html:
Prepayments are accruals' mirror: cash left early; expense belongs to the future. The tool is a schedule — build one:

March 1: Bellamy pays annual rent ₦2,400,000 for Mar–Feb. The payment posts Dr Prepaid Rent (asset) 2,400,000, Cr Bank. The schedule (its home per house convention — a sheet filed to the Hub, referenced in the playbook):

ItemPaidTotalMonthlyReleased to date (Jul)Balance
Rent Mar26–Feb2701-032,400,000200,0005 × 200,000 = 1,000,0001,400,000
Insurance Jun26–May2705-06360,00030,0002 × 30,000 = 60,000300,000

Every month-end, one mechanical journal per schedule line: Dr Rent Expense 200,000, Cr Prepaid Rent 200,000 (and Dr Insurance 30,000, Cr Prepaid Insurance 30,000). The month-end tick "accruals & prepayments posted" asserts these releases ran and the ledger's prepaid balances equal the schedule's balances — that equality is the control; when they diverge, someone released twice, skipped a month, or posted a new prepayment without a schedule line.

New prepayments join the schedule the day they're posted, not at month end — the payment entry and the schedule line are one act. Part-year items pro-rate from their start date (insurance from 5 June still releases a full June month per house convention — red-pen this if the house pro-rates by days). And when a prepaid service is cancelled mid-term with a refund, the refund credits the prepaid asset, the schedule ends early, and remarks tell the story.

Why the fuss for a retail client: without releases, March shows rent of 2.4m and April–Feb show zero — every month's profit is fiction in a different direction, and the MD makes decisions on fiction. The schedule is ten minutes of setup buying twelve months of truth.

DRILL: August's release runs, then you notice July's was never posted. August 31 now needs: the normal August release AND July's catch-up — two lines or one ₦400,000 journal with remarks itemising both months? House style says itemise: one journal, two remark lines, schedule annotated. The balance control (ledger = schedule) is what caught it; that's the control doing its job.

lessons.title: The payroll journal — gross to net, in naira
lessons.html:
The salaries BANK line (M2a line 11) only clears net pay. The real event is the payroll journal on pay day, booking gross cost and splitting every deduction to its keeper. Bellamy, July: staff gross ₦1,800,000. From the payroll schedule: PAYE ₦162,000; pension — employee 8% ₦144,000, employer 10% ₦180,000; net pay ₦1,494,000. (Numbers illustrative — M3 owns the real computation rules; this lesson owns the POSTING.)

26-07 Payroll JournalDrCr
Salaries & Wages (expense — gross)1,800,000
Pension Expense (employer 10%)180,000
PAYE Payable (control)162,000
Pension Payable (control: 144,000 + 180,000)324,000

Check the shape: the P&L carries the TRUE employment cost (1,800,000 + 180,000 = 1,980,000); the controls carry everyone who is owed: staff (net), the state (PAYE), the PFAs (pension both legs).

Then the clearings, as the bank lines arrive: salaries batch ₦1,494,000 → Dr Net Salaries Payable, Cr Bank (wait — the worked statement showed 1,420,000; a ₦74,000 gap means someone's net was held back or paid separately — reconcile the batch to the schedule, don't shrug); PAYE remittance by the 10th → Dr PAYE Payable 162,000, Cr Bank; pension remittance → Dr Pension Payable 324,000, Cr Bank.

The monthly control check (feeds the FS checklist's "payroll booked" tick): after all clearings, each payroll control holds exactly the amounts not yet remitted — reconciled to the schedule. PAYE Payable showing ₦162,000 on Aug 15 says July's PAYE wasn't remitted: that is an M3 deadline already missed or missing from the bank — either way, loud, today, not at close.

Where the module runs payroll (ERPNext HR/Payroll), the Salary Slips generate this journal — your job shifts to VERIFYING it against the schedule and chasing the clearings; where payroll is a spreadsheet schedule, you post the journal above by hand. Either way, the tick means checked, not assumed.

DRILL: New hire mid-month; the schedule shows her gross ₦150,000 pro-rated to ₦75,000, PAYE ₦4,200, pension EE ₦6,000/ER ₦7,500. Extend each journal line mentally: gross +75,000; ER pension expense +7,500; PAYE control +4,200; pension control +13,500; net +64,800. If the bank batch didn't grow by exactly 64,800, the batch-to-schedule reconciliation finds who wasn't paid.

lessons.title: Control accounts — reconciling, and diagnosing a broken one
lessons.html:
A control account's balance must always be DERIVABLE from a schedule outside the ledger. Monthly, you prove it. The VAT control, worked:

VAT Payable control — July₦
Opening balance (June's net, remitted 21-07)861,000 Cr
− Remittance 21-07 (M2a line 10)861,000 Dr → 0
+ Output VAT on July sales (per sales/Z summary)1,230,000 Cr
− Input VAT on eligible July purchases (per purchase summary)340,000 Dr
= Closing balance — and August's return890,000 Cr

The reconciliation: the LEDGER's control balance vs this DERIVED figure. Agreement → tick. Disagreement → diagnose before anything else ships. The diagnostic sequence for a control that's out by ₦37,500:

  1. Direction first: control higher than derived = something credited VAT that shouldn't have (a receipt mis-split? unidentified income parked as sales+VAT?); lower = output missed (a Z-report day unposted?) or input overclaimed.
  2. Round-number instinct: 37,500 = 7.5% of exactly 500,000 — hunt for a ₦500,000 transaction treated VAT-wrong: an exempt supply charged VAT, or a VATable sale posted VAT-free.
  3. Ledger walk: filter the control's period entries; every line must trace to an invoice batch, Z-report, or the remittance. The stranger is usually visible in one pass.
  4. Fix by the honest shape (reverse + repost, cross-referenced), re-derive, agree, THEN tick.

The same discipline serves every control: PAYE and pension to the payroll schedule (L4); WHT both directions to their certificate schedules — WHT receivable (withheld from us) grows with each shortfall-allocation (M2a L3) and shrinks when certificates are applied against tax; WHT payable (we withheld) grows with supplier splits (M2a L4) and zeroes at each remittance. A control that "roughly agrees" doesn't agree; and a control plugged to agree is a lie with compound interest — next month it's out by two mysteries instead of one.

Why the client's life depends on this: the money in these accounts is not the client's. A VAT control quietly treated as cash flow is how small businesses die owing FIRS money they already spent; our monthly reconciliation is the tripwire that keeps that truth visible in every pack.

DRILL: Pension Payable shows ₦324,000 on Aug 20; the schedule says July's remittance was due and the bank shows no pension line. What do you do, in order? Flag to the client TODAY (a missed statutory remittance, penalties accruing), note it for the reviewer, and do NOT clear or adjust the control — it is correctly reporting an unpaid debt. The control being "ugly" is the control WORKING.

lessons.title: Flux review — reading the month like a story
lessons.html:
After adjustments, before the pack: this month's P&L against last month's, line by line, and every material movement earns a one-sentence explanation IN WRITING (the checklist notes). Bellamy, July vs June:

LineJuneJulyΔYour sentence
Revenue9,840,00010,450,000+6%"Two new corporate accounts (Adebayo scale-up) — consistent with receipts."
Cost of sales5,610,0006,620,000+18%"Kolawole price increase from PO 118 + volume. Margin fell 3pts — flag to MD."
Electricity124,000247,300+99%STOP — investigate before writing anything.
Bank charges18,90031,400+66%"POS commission scaling with card mix — playbook rate confirms."
Repairs0230,000new"Generator repair (the Musa Ent query, resolved)."

The electricity line demonstrates the method's value: 99% is not a story, it's an alarm. Investigation finds the missed accrual reversal (L2's drill) — fixed BEFORE delivery, cheaply. The flux is where wrong postings are caught while they cost a journal entry instead of a restatement and an awkward client call.

What counts as material is a house threshold (red-pen: suggest greater of ₦50,000 or 15% of the line) — but judgment overrides thresholds in both directions: a ₦20,000 movement in a line that should NEVER move (statutory penalties: any amount is a story) matters; a ₦300,000 swing in a line that always swings (fuel, for a logistics client) may need only "seasonal, consistent with route volume".

Balance-sheet flux too, briefly: receivables jumping while revenue is flat = collections slipping (aging schedule tells who); inventory climbing against flat sales = the stock-take conversation; director loan movements = are the L6/M2a-line-12 answers consistent with what the account now says? The balance sheet is where quiet problems live; give it five minutes of the same reading.

Write the sentences INTO the checklist notes as you go — when the MD calls asking "why is cost of sales up?", the answer is already composed, calm, and consistent with what the reviewer read. A flux done in your head serves nobody at 5pm Friday.

DRILL: Revenue +2%, receivables +34%, cash −20%. Compose the one sentence this pattern demands, and name who hears it first. "Sales are steady but collections have slipped — top five aged debtors attached; suggest a collections push." The MD hears it — in the pack's cover note, flagged by the reviewer first.

lessons.title: The pack — producing, filing, delivering
lessons.html:
With postings current (attested), banks reconciled (filed), suspense zero, adjustments in, controls agreed, flux written — the pack is a harvest. The standard monthly pack (identical structure every client; only numbers differ):

  1. Profit & Loss — the period, with prior-month comparative (ERPNext financial statements report: period July, comparison previous period; house template governs layout).
  2. Balance Sheet — as at period end.
  3. Supporting schedules per house template — receivables aging, payables aging, bank summary (per account: opening, movements, closing, reconciled ✓). [Red-pen: confirm the canonical schedule list.]
  4. The cover note — five lines maximum: the month in one sentence, the two flux stories that matter, anything awaiting the client (open queries, the stock-take date). Written from the flux notes, not composed fresh.

Production mechanics: run the reports with the right dimensions/company, export to the house PDF template, and READ THE PDF — the render is what the client sees, and a truncated column or wrong comparative caught here costs a re-export; caught by the client, it costs credibility.

The delivery sequence, exactly (M1 L6 walked the ceremony; this is your checklist-side view): every checklist item ticked honestly → PDF filed to the Hub first (the ceremony must never point at an empty shelf) → In Review where a reviewer exists, with your doubts flagged in notes → the reviewer's Delivered → the client's 📬 → Acknowledged ✓✓. All inside the 5th working day.

When you'll miss the date — a client's statement page still missing on the 4th working day despite chases: the bad-news protocol (M4) runs BEFORE the deadline: the client hears "statements will be one day late because the GTB pages for the 28th–31st are outstanding — may we have them today?" from you, with the date, before the matrix tells them with a red cell. A miss announced early with its cause attached costs a day; a silent miss costs the thing the pack exists to build.

The pack that arrives on time, reconciled, with a cover note that answers the MD's question before it's asked, every single month — that is the entire brand of this unit. There is no marketing better than a client who has stopped checking whether the statements will come.

DRILL: It's the 3rd working day. Checklist shows 6/7 (reviewer pending), Hub has the PDF, one query from the 28th sits Answered-unresolved. What's left, in order? Resolve the query (repost + resolve — it may touch the numbers!), re-check the affected statements, re-file the PDF if changed, THEN In Review. Answered-unresolved before a close is a landmine with a polite label.

m4.title: Bookkeeper — The Professional Bookkeeper
m4.desc: Confidentiality with scenarios, the client voice with verbatim rewrites, the bad-news protocol, both chairs of review, and reading your own numbers.

lessons.title: Confidentiality — the walls, tested
lessons.html:
Every client room is a sealed vessel; the rules are absolute because the temptations are ordinary. Four scenarios, decided:

1. The benchmark request. Cascade's MD, friendly, over a call: "You do Bellamy too — what do retailers like them spend on POS charges? Just a range." The range IS Bellamy's data wearing a disguise. Answer from public knowledge only ("card commissions in Nigeria typically run 0.5–0.75%; let's look at YOURS") — and note the refusal shape: give something useful and general, so the no doesn't feel like a wall.

2. The helpful shortcut. Chidinma (Bellamy's bookkeeper-side contact) WhatsApps you asking for last month's P&L "quickly, the MD is asking". The document is theirs; the CHANNEL is the breach. "Sending it to your Documents now — it'll be in the portal in one minute." Client materials travel the logged rails even when the recipient is entitled to them; a personal-channel habit, once formed, will eventually carry something it must not.

3. The dinner story. A client's books contained something genuinely funny, no names needed. Not told. Lagos, at the level our clients live, is one degree of separation — and the storyteller who is careful with names is still teaching the table that our clients' insides are entertainment. The reputation cost lands on the unit, not the anecdote.

4. The device. Statements and exports on your laptop are transit, not archive: they live in the Hub, and local copies go when the task does. Screens lock when you stand; client tabs close before screen-shares; and the household rule applies — family seeing a client's name on your screen is already a leak, however loving the household.

Confidentiality is not a policy we comply with; it is the product. Clients hand us the most private thing a business has, and the fee is paid because the handover is safe. The breach that ends a career is rarely dramatic — a screenshot to the wrong chat, an open laptop, a story told well. Boring discipline is the whole game.

DRILL: A prospective client asks, as a test: "Who else do you keep books for?" What may you say? House policy [red-pen]: named references only with the referenced client's standing consent; otherwise sector-level ("retail, food, logistics") and the offer to arrange a reference call. The instinct to impress with names is the instinct to manage.

lessons.title: The client voice — five rewrites, verbatim
lessons.html:
To your clients you ARE the firm; every message teaches them what the service is like. The register: warm, plain, unhurried, never defensive; help-shaped, never accusation-shaped. Five real situations, bad and good, word for word:

1. The unexplained transaction.
✗ "You didn't tell us what the 230k cheque to Musa Ent was for. We can't do your books like this."
✓ "Could you help us place one item — a cheque to Musa Ent, ₦230,000, on the 9th? Once we know what it was for, July is fully posted."
The good version asks for help, names the specifics, and shows the payoff of answering.

2. The chronically late statement.
✗ "As usual we still don't have your GTB statement."
✓ "We're one document away from starting your close — the GTB statement for July. Could Tunde send it today? The earlier it lands, the earlier your statements do."
"As usual" wins an argument and loses a client; the good version converts frustration into a deadline the client can act on.

3. The client who wants the impossible.
✗ "That's not how accounting works."
✓ "There's a cleaner way to get what you're after. If we post it the way you've described, your VAT return overstates — which costs you real money. Here's what I'd suggest instead…"
Never make the client feel foolish; make the better path feel like THEIR win (because it is).

4. The scope drift.
✗ "We don't do that."
✓ "Happy to help with that — it sits outside your current service, so let me have our team add it properly with a small fee adjustment. That way it's covered every month, not just this once."
The no becomes a yes-with-structure; the tier conversation (M1) in its natural habitat.

5. The angry message. Client, 21:40: "Third time asking about this!!! Is anyone actually working on our account???"
✗ (at 21:41) "We replied on Tuesday, please check your portal."
✓ (next working morning, 08:40) "You're right to expect better tracking from us, and I'm sorry this felt dropped. Here's where each of your three items stands: [three lines]. The second one is waiting on the bank's response — I'll chase them this morning and update you by noon."
Note everything the good version does: waits for working hours (the after-hours notice covered the night; answering at 21:41 teaches a service level we don't sell), opens with validation not evidence, itemises, owns the next action WITH a time. You may be right on the facts and still wrong in the reply.

The channel rule underneath all five: queries through Follow-ups, documents through requests, everything else in the room — and any material thing settled by voice gets a same-day room summary, because a decision that exists only in a phone call doesn't exist.

DRILL: Rewrite this real specimen: "We noticed you again mixed personal and business spending. This makes our work very difficult." — One good answer: "A few July items look personal (list attached, ₦184,000 total) — should we treat these as drawings as before? If it helps, a separate card for business spend would make your statements cleaner and your tax position safer." Names the facts, offers the mechanism, gives the client a dignified path.

lessons.title: Bad news — the protocol, walked
lessons.html:
Something will eventually go wrong: a statement will be late, an error will reach a delivered pack, a statutory date will be at risk. The protocol is identical for all three: early, plainly, cause attached, path forward, before the system's surfaces tell them first.

Walk the late statement. It's the 4th working day; Bellamy's GTB pages for the 28th–31st are still missing despite two chases. The deadline is tomorrow and you will miss it. The message goes TODAY:

"Your July statements will be one day late — we're missing the GTB pages for the 28th–31st, which we've requested twice (most recently this morning). The moment they arrive we need about three hours; if Tunde can send them today, we may still make Friday. Everything else is closed and reviewed."

Anatomy: the news first (no burying), the cause (specific, not defensive), the client's lever (Tunde, today), the honest new promise, and the reassurance that is TRUE (the rest is done). What it never contains: "unfortunately due to circumstances", blame theatrics, or a promise you can't keep to soften the moment.

Walk the discovered error. August 12th, you find July's delivered pack overstated repairs by ₦230,000 (a suspense repost missed the reversal). The instinct to quietly fix it in August is the career-shaping mistake. The sequence: reviewer first (same hour), agreed correction, then the client — "We found an error in July's delivered statements: repairs were overstated by ₦230,000, profit correspondingly understated. Corrected statements are in your Documents; the cause was a duplicated posting on our side, and we've added a check so it can't recur." Clients forgive errors admitted at speed with corrections attached; they never forgive discovering one themselves.

Walk the statutory risk. The 19th, VAT due the 21st, and the client hasn't answered the query that determines ₦500,000 of output VAT. This one escalates INSIDE first (reviewer + books manager, today) because the decision — file on best evidence vs file late — is a management call with penalty mathematics attached; the client message then carries the firm's decision, not your improvisation.

The invariant: the client must never learn of a problem from a red cell, a silent gap, or their own discovery. The board's surfaces are fast; you must be faster, and the difference between "they told me before I asked" and "I found out" is, over a few years, the difference between a reference and a churn.

DRILL: Which is worse: statements two days late and announced on day one, or one day late and silent? — Silent, and it isn't close. Lateness costs a day; silence costs the belief that you'd tell them. The entire acknowledgment/ceremony machinery is built on that belief.

lessons.title: Review — both chairs, with a worked exchange
lessons.html:
On split clients one prepares, one signs. Here is a real review cycle done well, then the crafts named.

The submission (you, preparer): Cascade July → In Review, notes: "Checklist 6/7. Flux notes in the cell. Two things for your eye: (1) director loan repostings wk3 — I followed his email but the pattern's new; (2) COGS +18% — I've verified Kolawole's price letter, but the margin drop deserves your read before it reaches the MD." — The craft: review-ready state (suspense zero, notes written) plus your own doubts flagged, not buried. A preparer who surfaces doubts is trusted more; a reviewer who finds an UNFLAGGED known-issue trusts everything less, permanently.

The findings (Ade, reviewer): "Two findings. (1) Rent release doubled — March's reversal missing; fix and re-lay the P&L (this also resolves half your COGS-margin worry: ₦200k of it isn't COGS at all, it's the rent error's shadow in the comparative). (2) Director loan treatment is right, but add his email to the Hub as support. Everything else clean — the flux notes are exactly what the MD conversation needs." — The craft: findings with REASONS and locations ("March's reversal"), teaching not verdicts; credit where due; the fix's downstream effect traced. Compare the useless version: "redo the rent figures and tidy the loan section."

The response (you): fix, re-lay, re-file, one line back: "Both done — reversal posted (JE-00318), P&L re-laid, email filed. Re-review when ready." Never relitigate the fact of being checked; argue the ACCOUNTING when you disagree ("I read the pro-ration differently — here's the contract clause") and accept the outcome when the reviewer holds.

The signature (Ade): reviewer-pass tick, Delivered. That click means "I believe these statements" — which is why review is substance (recs to statements, controls to schedules, flux against knowledge of the client) and never a checklist skim. And it is PROMPT: work at In Review since the 3rd deserves better than a signature on the 7th; the 👁 push exists so the handover never waits on memory.

The culture line: the gate only works if being reviewed carries no shame and reviewing carries no superiority. The best pairs swap findings like colleagues sharpening each other — because that is what they are. And the SM override on the gate is for genuine emergencies; a pattern of overrides is a pattern management reads correctly.

DRILL: As reviewer you find a third consecutive month of the same suspense-hygiene issue from the same preparer. The finding goes in the review — where else does the observation belong? A direct conversation (kind, specific, offline from the artifact) — findings fix statements; conversations fix patterns. If a third conversation doesn't, the books manager should hear it from you before the KPIs say it anyway.

lessons.title: Your numbers — reading the board without flinching
lessons.html:
The board measures the work: on-time rate, posting lags, close cycles, register dots, and (for managers) each engagement's effective hourly rate. Professionals read their own numbers the way they read a client's: honestly, hunting the story. A sample read:

Your six-month row: on-time 94% → 91% → 96% → 88% → 90% → 84%. FS cycle: 4.2d → 4.5d → 4.1d → 5.8d → 5.5d → 6.3d. The story isn't "getting worse at the job" — cross-reference capacity: you went from 3 clients to 5 in month four. The honest conclusion is a LOAD conversation with the books manager, armed with the numbers ("my cycle degraded exactly when the portfolio grew — I'm at capacity, or my rhythm needs redesign, or both"). The board wrote your case for you; that is what it's for.

The two corruptions, named: Gaming — attesting optimistically, back-dating effort, ticking unverified — poisons the board for everyone and is a short strategy against a system whose cross-checks (sessions vs claims, batch vs schedule, and one day the ledger itself) have a long memory. Despair — treating an amber month as a verdict — misreads what the numbers are: descriptions of the service each client received, nothing more. The correct response to a bad number is curiosity (what in my rhythm produced this?) followed by a changed rhythm.

The fee-review flag, understood precisely: when an engagement runs below the rate floor three straight months, the CLIENT is flagged — for repricing, not for blame. It means the engagement is bigger than the fee assumed. Your honest hours are the evidence that makes the repricing case; understating hours to look efficient literally hides money the unit should be earning. The flag firing is the pricing system WORKING.

Capacity and growth: the lightest-honest-load table assigns the next client; disciplined numbers are how growth lands fairly, and how your advancement case gets written by the board instead of by adjectives. The closing loop of this whole track: tag sessions, attest truly, raise queries the day you hit them, tick what you verified — do the disciplines and the KPIs take care of themselves. That is the design.

DRILL: Your Cascade rate reads ₦3,900/hr for the third month; the flag fires. A colleague suggests logging fewer Cascade hours "so it looks better". Name the three things wrong with that in one breath: it hides an underpriced engagement (unit loses money), corrupts capacity planning (you'll be assigned MORE work), and it's a falsified record in a system built on attestation. The right move: nothing — the flag is doing your negotiating for you.
